knowledge_point.title: Applying Green's Theorem to Regions With Holes: Advanced Cases

question.:question/problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/edb-math/repairs/2026-10-28-topic-audit-3/published-probe/17592186133900/17592186133900/c7bbe738a0c044dadfc62bde3cfb22aebb86d9491e2b957eef66f85a34e86fdb.png)

Given $\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}=x^{2} + y^{2}$, calculate 

$$
\oint_{\partial D}P\,\mathrm dx+Q\,\mathrm dy
$$

 over the positively oriented annular region shown above.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Green's theorem can be extended to include regions containing holes. In such cases, we can apply Green's theorem in the same way as before.

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\oint_{\partial D}P\,\mathrm dx+Q\,\mathrm dy & =\iint_D x^{2} + y^{2}\,\mathrm dA.\end{aligned}
$$

The region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as 

$$
\Delta=\{(r,\theta):2\le r\le 5,0\le\theta\le2\pi\}.
$$

Recall that the change of variables formula for polar coordinates gives

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, our double integral becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_D x^{2} + y^{2}\,\mathrm dA & =\int_{0}^{2 \pi}\int_{2}^{5}((r\cos\theta)^2+(r\sin\theta)^2)\cdot r\,\mathrm d r\,\mathrm d \theta\\ & =\int_{0}^{2 \pi}\int_{2}^{5}r^{2}(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta)\cdot r\,\mathrm d r\,\mathrm d \theta\\ & =\int_{0}^{2 \pi}\int_{2}^{5}r^{3}\,\mathrm d r\,\mathrm d \theta\\ & =\int_{0}^{2 \pi}\,\mathrm d \theta\cdot \int_{2}^{5}r^{3}\,\mathrm d r\\ & =2 \pi\cdot \int_{2}^{5}r^{3}\,\mathrm d r\\ & =2 \pi\cdot \frac{r^{4}}{4}\big|_{2}^{5}\\ & =2 \pi\cdot (\left(\frac{625}{4}\right)-\left(4\right))\\ & =\frac{\pi}{2}\cdot \left((5)^{4}-\left((2)^{4}\right)\right)\\ & =\frac{\pi}{2}\cdot \left(625-\left(16\right)\right)\\ & =\frac{609 \pi}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
